phonemes.desc: Close front [i] followed by voiceless postalveolar fricative [ʃ] — the Akkadian rendering of the Sumerian divine name.
Voiceless dental [t] and syllabic [ar] — the second element, possibly connected with 'morning star' or simply the borrowing of Inanna.

pronunciation.approximation: 'EESH-tar' — the š is like the sh in 'ship,' and the final syllable is slightly drawn out.

pronunciation.note: Ištar is Tier 1 because the caron on š marks the Akkadian sibilant — a distinctive feature the ASCII form loses. The macron form Ištār is sometimes used to mark an optional or dialectal length, but the primary cuneiform evidence supports /ˈiʃtar/; the Unicode form Ištar is therefore the transparent, historically defensible spelling, with the caron š marking the Akkadian sibilant.

domains.title: Lady of Heaven
domains.subtitle: Love, War, Fertility, Venus
domains.lead: Ištar is the most volatile of the great Mesopotamian goddesses. She is the planet Venus, the morning and evening star; she is sexual desire and reproductive power; she is the frenzy of battle and the protector of kings. No other deity in the ancient Near East so thoroughly unites what later cultures would separate into Aphrodítē and Árēs.

cards.name: The Star
cards.desc: The eight-pointed star of Venus; Ištar is the brightest planet and the celestial sign of the goddess.

cards.name: Love and Fertility
cards.desc: The sacred marriage, the life-giving womb, the power that turns desire into offspring and fields into harvest.

cards.name: War
cards.desc: She rides into battle with weapons at her shoulders; kings claim her as their divine patron in war.

cards.name: Lions and Doves
cards.desc: The lion is her warlike aspect; the dove is her amorous aspect — power and tenderness in one deity.

symbols.name: Eight-pointed star
symbols.meaning: Venus and the celestial throne of the goddess; the star writes her name in cuneiform

symbols.name: Lion
symbols.meaning: War, royal power, and the dangerous side of desire; she strides upon lions on cylinder seals

symbols.name: Dove
symbols.meaning: Love, sexuality, and the goddess's eastern cult

symbols.name: Rosette
symbols.meaning: Fertility and the blooming of life, attached to her cult from the Uruk-period seals onward

symbols.name: Weapons on shoulders
symbols.meaning: The warrior goddess armed for battle — bows, maces, and quivers strapped across her back

symbols.name: Inanna's knot
symbols.meaning: The looped reed-bundle or gatepost emblem on Uruk-period seals — the oldest sign of her sovereignty at her cult city

mythology.lead: Ištar's myths are stories of extremity: descent into death, demand for the impossible, and the transformation of gender and power. She is never merely an object of desire; she is desire in motion, war in motion, the star that crosses the boundary between heaven and the underworld.

myths.title: Inanna's Descent to the Underworld
myths.text: In the Sumerian Descent of Inanna (ETCSL 1.4.1) and its Akkadian retelling, the Descent of Ishtar, the goddess abandons heaven and earth to descend to the netherworld ruled by her sister Ereškigal. At each of the seven gates the porter strips her of a garment or ornament — crown, beads, robe, until she stands naked before the throne of the dead. The Anunnaki fasten on her 'the eye of death'; she is killed and hung on a hook. Her faithful servant Ninšubur pleads at the great gods' doors until Enki fashions two sexless beings who slip past Ereškigal's grief and revive Inanna with the food and water of life. The price of her return is a substitute, and her own husband Dumuzi is sent down in her place. The myth means that descent is survivable but not free: everything that goes down must be ransomed by something of equal value.

myths.title: Ištar and the Bull of Heaven
myths.text: In Tablet VI of the Epic of Gilgamesh, Ištar proposes marriage to Gilgameš, king of Uruk — who answers with the most impudent speech in the epic, cataloguing the fates of her previous lovers: Dumuzi, doomed to the underworld year after year; the shepherd, changed into a wolf; the horse, driven to death; and the gardener Išullanu, turned into a frog. Enraged, Ištar ascends to heaven and demands the Bull of Heaven from Anu, threatening to raise the dead to devour the living if refused. The bull descends on Uruk and kills hundreds with its snort before Gilgameš and Enkidu slay it — and Enkidu's ensuing death, decreed by the gods for the insult to Ištar, is the hinge on which the whole epic turns. The myth means that to refuse a goddess is to trigger a chain of consequences no hero can outrun.

myths.title: Dumuzi and Inanna
myths.text: The Sumerian sacred-marriage songs (especially the songs of Iddin-Dagan of Isin, ETCSL 2.5.3) celebrate the union of Inanna and Dumuzi, the shepherd-king: the goddess chooses the king as her bridegroom, and their lovemaking guarantees the fertility of the land and the legitimacy of his rule. But the Descent adds the darker clause: when Inanna needs a substitute in the netherworld, her gaze falls on Dumuzi, 'the young man for whom she had cried,' and he is dragged below — until his sister Geštinanna offers to share his exile, so that the two alternate half the year each. The cycle of presence and absence, presence and absence, becomes the rhythm of the agricultural year. The myth means that love and loss are not opposites but a seasonal alternation built into the world's contract.

myths.title: Ištar Annihilates Mount Ebih
myths.text: A hymn known in Old Babylonian and later recensions as Ištar and Ebih tells how the great mountain range refused to bow to the goddess — 'it did not revere me in glory, it did not set its neck to the ground.' Ištar, 'the queen of Heaven and Earth,' arms for war against the landscape itself: she demands weapons from Anu, marches on Ebih, and 'raised my torch, scorched the mountain, poured flame over it,' finishing by laying the rebellious range flat and flooding its valleys. The poem, long read as a hymn to Ištar of Agade's martial triumphs, works at two levels: the goddess's sovereignty extends even over geography, and insubordination — in a person or a mountain — is the one thing she never forgives. The myth means that her dominion is not a metaphor: the world itself is her subject.

myths.title: Ištar Abandons Ur
myths.text: The Sumerian city-laments — above all the Lament for Ur (ETCSL 2.2.2), mourning the city's sack by the Elamites around 2004 BCE — give Ištar/Inanna her most haunting role. Before the destruction she leaves her temple, 'like a bird she flew off,' and the city is stripped of its protecting goddess; the Elamite and Shimashki troops move through the unguarded streets while the moon sets on the empty shrines. After the catastrophe she returns and walks through the ruins weeping, while the lament's singer asks her to rebuild the destroyed shrines. The genre means something the love-and-war epics never say plainly: a goddess can leave, and when she leaves, the walls, the canals, and the granaries are all just bricks and dust. Ištar's presence is the condition of the city's reality; her absence is its end.

lore.syncretism: Ištar absorbed the Sumerian Inanna so completely that the two are now treated as a single deity across the ancient Near East. She was identified with the Canaanite Astarte, the Hurrian Šauška, the Egyptian Qudshu, the Greek Aphrodítē (especially in her eastern, armed form), and the Persian Anahita. The Hellenistic cult of Aphrodite Ourania at Ascalon and elsewhere preserves strong Ištar/Astarte elements. In later Gnostic and magical texts, Ištar's star became an emblem of celestial femininity and erotic power.
lore.culturalLegacy: A popular claim derives English Easter from Ištar's name, but the derivation is not supported by scholarship: Bede explains the month-name Eosturmonath from a Germanic goddess Eostre, and no historical or linguistic chain connects Eostre with Ištar or Astarte; the resemblance is coincidence. Her genuine afterlife runs through the figure of the Whore of Babylon in the Book of Revelation and countless depictions of the love-and-war goddess. The Epic of Gilgamesh made her a byword for dangerous female desire, though the Sumerian sources present a far more complex figure. Her eight-pointed star survives in Islamic and occult iconography, and her lions and doves still decorate the borders between sexuality and power. The name still means: the star that crosses every boundary.
lore.extendedMeditation:
Ištar refuses to be one thing. She is the morning star and the evening star, the lover and the warrior, the goddess who descends into death and returns clothed in her own power. In a world that likes its deities sorted by function, she is a reminder that the most ancient sacred forces were polymorphous: desire and violence, fertility and mourning, all braided into a single brilliant light.

To restore the name Ištar is to refuse the flattening of the feminine divine into mere beauty or mere nurturing. She is the terror of the battlefield and the tenderness of the bridal chamber; the goddess who weeps over a ruined city and sends the Bull of Heaven to avenge her pride. Her star still rises. It still crosses from day into night, from life into death, and back again.

lore.archaeology: The glazed-brick Ishtar Gate, excavated at Babylon by Robert Koldewey and now in Berlin's Pergamon Museum, displays lions, aurochs, and mušḫuššu-dragons marking the goddess's processional way. At Uruk, the Eanna precinct preserves the sequence of Inanna temples from the Uruk period onward, source of the archaic seals that first display her star, lion, and rosette; at Assur, the Assyrian Ishtar temple yielded votive inscriptions of Sennacherib and Esarhaddon. Countless cylinder seals, terracotta plaques, and ivory panels show her as armed goddess, nude fertility figure, and eight-pointed star, and the Isin sacred-marriage hymns anchor her bridal cult in a datable royal liturgy.
